newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile's Frei welcomes end of drug case gag order.
newsitem.headline: Chile's Frei welcomes end of drug case gag order.

text.p: Chilean President Eduardo Frei on Friday welcomed a court decision to lift a 10-day gag order in a sensational drugs case, which a local newspaper had skirted by using the Internet.
"I am very pleased as it is good and fundamental that there is transparency in judicial cases," said Frei who last week criticized the decision to bar news media from reporting on the case.
An appeals court ruled unanimously on Thursday to lift the ban imposed by a judge who is investigating Chile's largest drug-trafficking and money laundering case.
The probe involves businessman Mario Silva Leiva who is accused of heading a multi-million-dollar drugs ring traffiking cocaine from Peru and Bolivia through Brazil to Europe.

Newspapers splashed front-page stories on the case on Friday including a report that investigators were considering seeking an order to force Swiss banks to return $10 million allegedly deposited in secret accounts by Leiva's relatives.
Newspaper La Tercera broke ground in Chile by opening a site on the World Wide Web last week to give readers the stories that were not published because of the court order.
"The country is (sufficiently) developed ... to assume the responsibility of being informed about the truth," said the director of La Tercera, Fernando Paulsen.

Leiva was one of 15 people arrested three months ago in what police called their biggest blow against the drug trade in Chile. Those implicated include a top court official who is accused of protecting Leiva.
The authorities also froze bank accounts worth more than $100 million in the case, which was a headline-grabbing story in Chile until the press blackout.
